# Fetch FIFO Behavioral Specification

## 1. Overview

The Fetch FIFO buffers instruction-fetch responses from a 32-bit memory interface and presents them to the instruction consumer as a stream of individual instructions. It supports both 32-bit RISC-V instructions and 16-bit compressed instructions. An instruction may begin at byte offset 0 or byte offset 2 within a fetched 32-bit word, and a 32-bit instruction beginning at byte offset 2 may span two fetched words.

A fetched word consists of:

- a halfword-aligned fetch-stream address associated with the fetched word,
- 32 bits of fetched instruction data,
- an error indication for that fetch.

## 2. Basic handshake behavior

### Reset and clear

- On reset, the module shall discard all buffered fetch words and reset its alignment state. No output shall be presented from stored FIFO state.
- A clear request shall invalidate all buffered fetch words and reset the half-word alignment state on the next clock edge.
- If a clear request and an input transfer occur in the same cycle, the input word shall also be discarded; clear takes priority over storing new data.
- A clear request does not necessarily suppress an output transfer in the same cycle. It defines the state after the current clock edge.

### Input port

- An input fetch word is accepted on a clock edge when both input valid and input ready are asserted in that cycle.
- The module shall assert input ready whenever it can accept a fetch word. A word accepted while clear is asserted is discarded rather than stored.

### Output port

- An output instruction is delivered on a clock edge when both output valid and output ready are asserted in that cycle.
- The module shall assert output valid only when it is presenting a complete instruction.
- Output validity shall be independent of the error flag. An instruction may be delivered with an error indication set.

## 3. Word and instruction alignment

The module uses RISC-V half-word ordering within each 32-bit fetch word:

- The half-word at byte offset 0 is in bits [15:0] of the fetched word.
- The half-word at byte offset 2 is in bits [31:16] of the fetched word.
- A half-word whose low two bits are `2'b11` is the first half of a 32-bit instruction.
- A half-word whose low two bits are not `2'b11` is a 16-bit compressed instruction.

The output address shall be half-word aligned. Bit 0 of the output address shall be 0. Bit 1 indicates whether the current instruction starts at byte offset 0 or byte offset 2 within the current fetched word.

When output valid is asserted:

- The low 16 bits of the output data contain the first half-word of the current instruction.
- For a 32-bit instruction, the high 16 bits contain the second half-word of the instruction.
- For a 16-bit instruction, only the low half-word is part of the current transfer; the high half-word is not consumed by this transfer.

## 4. Instruction delivery and retirement behavior

A fetched word is “available” if it is already buffered or if it is supplied by the input port in the current cycle.

The following behavior shall apply when an output transfer occurs:

| Current instruction start | Instruction size | Required data | After output transfer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Offset 0 | 16-bit compressed | Current word only | Current word is kept. The next instruction starts at offset 2 within the same word. |
| Offset 0 | 32-bit | Current word only | Current word is retired. The next instruction starts at offset 0 of the next word. |
| Offset 2 | 16-bit compressed | Current word, upper half-word | Current word is retired. The next instruction starts at offset 0 of the next word. |
| Offset 2 | 32-bit | Current word upper half-word and next word lower half-word | Current word is retired. The next word is kept and becomes the current word. The next instruction starts at offset 2 of that word. |

The module shall not present a partial instruction. In particular, for a 32-bit instruction starting at offset 2, output valid shall remain low until both the current word and the following word are available.

Retiring a word means it is no longer buffered and will not be presented again. Keeping a word means it remains buffered for subsequent instruction delivery.

## 5. Error handling

Each fetched word carries its own error indication. The error output for a delivered instruction shall be:

- For a 16-bit compressed instruction: the error indication of the single word containing that instruction.
- For a 32-bit instruction starting at offset 0: the error indication of that word.
- For a 32-bit instruction starting at offset 2 and spanning two words: the logical OR of the error indications of both contributing words.

If a word remains buffered for use by a later instruction, its error indication shall remain associated with it. If one contributing word is supplied directly by the input port, that word’s error indication shall be included in the error output for that instruction.

# Instruction Fetch Stage Specification

## 1. Overview

The instruction fetch stage is responsible for supplying the instruction stream to the rest of the core. It selects the next instruction address, performs instruction fetch requests to the instruction memory or cache, handles instruction data returned by the memory system, expands compressed instructions, and presents one decoded/expanded instruction to the decode stage.

The stage must be able to deliver one instruction per cycle when the memory system and decode stage allow it. To hide memory latency, it may fetch and buffer instructions ahead of the instruction currently being delivered.

## 2. Reset and Initialization

After reset, the instruction visible to the decode stage shall be invalid, and no instruction shall be considered newly available.

Once instruction fetching is enabled, the stage shall start fetching from the boot PC. The boot PC shall be the boot address plus `0x80`. The boot address input must be aligned to 256 bytes.

The boot address is also used as the initial trap-vector base. When the boot PC selection is made, the stage shall assert a request to initialize the trap-vector base register with the boot address.

## 3. Fetch Target Selection

When a PC change is requested, the stage shall redirect the fetch stream to the selected target immediately. Any instruction fetched from the old instruction stream shall not be delivered after the redirect.

The stage shall support the following target selections:

- **Boot**: fetch from the boot PC.
- **Taken jump or branch**: fetch from the supplied jump/branch target address.
- **Synchronous exception**: fetch from the trap-vector base, with the low 8 bits of the trap-vector base forced to zero.
- **Interrupt**: fetch from the trap-vector base plus an interrupt vector offset. The offset shall be the interrupt identifier multiplied by 4. The interrupt identifier is derived from the low bits of the exception cause.
- **Debug halt**: fetch from the configured debug halt address.
- **Debug exception**: fetch from the configured debug exception address.
- **Exception return**: fetch from the saved exception return PC.
- **Debug return**: fetch from the saved debug return PC.

The debug halt and debug exception addresses are configuration parameters. In the default configuration, the debug halt address is `0x1A110800` and the debug exception address is `0x1A110808`.

## 4. Instruction Fetch and Memory Interface

The stage shall perform instruction fetch reads using word-aligned addresses. The low two bits of the externally presented instruction address shall be zero.

The fetch interface uses a request/grant/response protocol:

- A fetch request shall be asserted whenever the stage needs to read an instruction word.
- The request shall remain asserted until the memory system accepts it with a grant.
- The address may change while a request is pending, for example due to a branch or exception redirect. The memory system must associate the returned data with the address that was present at the time of grant.
- A response valid pulse indicates that the instruction data and any error qualifiers on that cycle belong to the granted fetch request.
- A granted fetch request may receive its response one or more cycles after the grant.
- A grant presented when no fetch request is active shall have no effect on the fetch state.
- A response-valid indication shall be processed only when a previously granted fetch request is outstanding. A spurious response-valid indication with no outstanding request shall be ignored.
- Sequential fetch-address state shall advance only when the corresponding request is accepted with a grant.

The stage shall only ever present word-aligned fetch addresses to the memory system. Internally, the stage may deal with half-word-aligned instruction addresses to support compressed instructions. If an instruction spans or is offset within a fetched word, the stage shall use one or more word-aligned fetches as needed and select the appropriate instruction internally.

## 5. Instruction Delivery to the Decode Stage

The stage maintains a decode-visible instruction slot. This slot holds the instruction currently presented to the decode stage along with its associated metadata.

A new instruction shall be loaded into the decode-visible slot when all of the following conditions are true:

- a fetched instruction is available from the fetch stream,
- instruction fetching is enabled,
- the decode stage is ready to accept an instruction.

When a new instruction is loaded:

- the valid indicator shall be set,
- the new-instruction indicator shall be asserted for that cycle,
- the instruction data, instruction PC, compressed flags, and error flags shall be updated.

If the decode stage is not ready, no new instruction shall be loaded. The currently held instruction shall remain stable and valid.

The valid indicator, once set, shall remain asserted until one of the following occurs:

- an explicit invalidate request is honored,
- the slot is overwritten by a new instruction.

An explicit invalidate request shall clear the valid indicator unless a new instruction is being loaded in the same cycle. If a new instruction is loaded in the same cycle, the invalidate request shall be ignored.

A PC change request shall suppress delivery of any instruction fetched from the old stream. A PC change alone shall not modify the valid indicator of the decode-visible slot; that slot is only updated by a new-instruction load or an explicit invalidate.

## 6. Compressed Instruction Support

The stage shall determine whether each fetched instruction is a 32-bit instruction or a 16-bit compressed instruction.

For a 32-bit instruction:

- the compressed-instruction indicator shall be deasserted,
- the instruction data presented to decode shall be the 32-bit instruction.

For a compressed instruction:

- the compressed-instruction indicator shall be asserted,
- the instruction shall be expanded to its 32-bit equivalent before being presented to decode,
- the original 16-bit compressed encoding shall also be provided.

If a compressed encoding does not correspond to a legal compressed instruction, the stage shall set the illegal-compressed-instruction indicator. The instruction shall still be delivered so that the core can raise the appropriate exception.

## 7. Instruction Fetch Errors

The stage shall capture memory access errors associated with a fetched instruction, including bus errors and physical memory protection errors.

When a fetch error is present:

- the instruction shall still be marked valid and delivered to the decode stage,
- the fetch-error indicator for that instruction shall be asserted.

This allows the core to raise an instruction access fault exception based on the fetched instruction. When no error is present, the fetch-error indicator shall be deasserted.

## 8. Address Outputs

The stage shall provide an address for the instruction currently at the head of the fetch stream. This represents the next instruction that can enter the decode-visible slot.

The stage shall also provide the address of the instruction currently in the decode-visible slot. This address shall be captured when the instruction is loaded and shall remain constant while that instruction is held due to a stall.

## 9. Status and Performance Indication

The stage shall provide a busy status indicating that it is actively fetching instructions from the memory system.

The stage shall also provide an instruction-fetch miss performance event. This event shall be asserted when the fetch stream is not providing a valid fetched instruction at the point it is needed, or when a fetch redirect occurs and the currently buffered fetch stream is discarded.

# Behavioral Specification: Instruction Prefetch Buffer

## 1. Overview

The prefetch buffer issues word-aligned memory fetches and supplies an instruction-aligned stream to the core through its internal fetch FIFO. The output may represent a compressed instruction or a 32-bit instruction assembled from one or two fetched words. The module improves performance by allowing a limited number of fetches to remain in flight and by buffering completed responses. A branch redirects the fetch stream and discards earlier speculative fetch state.

## 2. Reset and Initial State

On reset, the prefetch buffer shall:

- discard all buffered fetch data;
- clear all outstanding-request and branch-abort tracking;
- clear any saved unaccepted-request and address-hold state;
- not present a valid response from stored state.

When no new fetch is requested, the request and busy outputs shall be deasserted after reset. These outputs are not required to remain deasserted if current input conditions request a new fetch.

## 3. Core Instruction Output

The prefetch buffer presents fetched words to the core using a valid/ready flow-control scheme:

- When the output is valid, the output word, its associated address, and its error status are meaningful.
- The output word, address, and error status must remain stable until the core accepts it.
- Once accepted, the prefetch buffer may present the next buffered word in the same or a later cycle.
- Fetched words must be presented in the same order as they complete in the fetch stream.
- A branch cancels any currently offered or buffered word from the old stream, even if the core has not yet accepted it.

The output represents an instruction-aligned stream produced by the internal fetch FIFO. A compressed instruction occupies the low halfword of the output data, while a 32-bit instruction may be assembled from two adjacent fetched words. The associated output address identifies the current instruction and may be word-aligned or halfword-aligned. The address associated with each output word indicates the fetch-stream address for that word.

## 4. Fetch Request Generation

The prefetch buffer issues word-aligned read requests to the instruction memory/cache interface.

- A request is made when there is fetch demand and the prefetch buffer has capacity for another outstanding transaction.
- If the memory interface does not accept a request, the request must remain asserted and the request address must remain stable, except for a branch redirect.
- Once a request is accepted, it becomes an outstanding transaction. The prefetch buffer may issue a new request in a subsequent cycle if there is demand and capacity.
- The prefetch buffer must not issue a new request while the maximum number of outstanding transactions is already reached.
- The prefetch buffer must not issue more than one request on the request/address output at the same time.
- Once asserted, an unaccepted request shall remain asserted until it is granted.
- The address of an unaccepted request shall remain stable, except when a branch redirects the pending request.
- Internal sequential-address state shall advance only when a request is accepted with `instr_gnt_i`.
- A request that has not been granted shall not cause the stored fetch address to advance.

## 5. Memory Response Handling

Each accepted request eventually produces a response. The prefetch buffer shall:

- associate the returned data/error with the next outstanding fetch in order;
- deliver the fetched word to the core in the same order as the corresponding requests;
- not present response data for a request that has been canceled by a branch;
- forward a memory error to the core as an error on the affected fetched word.
- `instr_rvalid_i` shall be processed only when a previously granted fetch request is outstanding.
- A spurious `instr_rvalid_i` indication when no request is outstanding shall not advance the fetch address or assert output validity.

The data returned with an error response is not meaningful but may be supplied alongside the error status.

## 6. Address Generation and Alignment

The prefetch buffer normally fetches sequential word addresses:

- After a fetch for one word, the next sequential fetch address is the next word-aligned address.
- The address presented on the memory request interface must be word-aligned.
- The address presented to the core with a fetched word is the fetch-stream address. For normal sequential fetches, this matches the word-aligned memory address.
- When a branch targets a half-word-aligned address, the memory request is for the word containing that target. The output address for the resulting fetched word may be the half-word-aligned fetch-stream address.

## 7. Branch Behavior

When a branch is taken with a new target address:

- Any request currently presented but not yet accepted shall be redirected to the branch target.
- Previously buffered data from the old fetch stream shall be invalidated when the FIFO clear takes effect.
- An old-stream output may remain combinationally visible during the branch cycle, but the consumer shall give the branch redirect priority over that output.
- Earlier accepted requests whose responses have not yet arrived shall be marked for discard, but they shall remain outstanding until their responses arrive.
- Responses from discarded requests, including error responses, shall be consumed without being inserted into the redirected instruction stream.
- The prefetch buffer shall resume fetching from the word containing the branch target when request capacity is available.
- If all outstanding-request slots are occupied, the branch-target request may have to wait until an earlier response frees a slot.
- No data or error from the old fetch stream shall be presented as part of the redirected stream after the FIFO clear takes effect.

## 8. Error Behavior

### 8.1 Memory Errors

If the memory interface reports an error for a transaction, the prefetch buffer shall present that transaction to the core with the error status asserted. The error is part of the normal fetch stream and shall respect stream ordering.

### 8.2 PMP Errors

If a fetch address fails a physical memory protection (PMP) check:

- The prefetch buffer shall not wait for a real memory data response for that address.
- It shall still complete the fetch as an internal transaction and present an error status to the core for that address.
- The error shall appear at the correct position in the fetch stream.
- A PMP error must not prevent later valid fetch requests from proceeding.
- A PMP error may be canceled by a branch in the same way as any other buffered fetched word.

## 9. Maximum Outstanding Transactions

The prefetch buffer may have at most two outstanding memory transactions waiting for responses. This limit includes PMP-error transactions that do not require a real memory response. While the limit is reached:

- no new memory request shall be issued;
- the prefetch buffer may continue presenting already buffered words to the core;
- a new request may only be issued after an outstanding transaction completes and frees a request slot;
- a branch marks earlier transactions for discard but does not free their request slots before their responses arrive.

## 10. Busy/Status Behavior

The busy output shall indicate whether the prefetch buffer is active on the memory interface:

- Busy shall be asserted when a memory request is currently being presented or when one or more outstanding memory transactions have not yet completed.
- Busy shall be deasserted when there is no active request being presented and no outstanding transaction.
- Busy does not indicate whether fetched data is available to the core; it only reflects memory interface activity.
